content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses dataset bias in NLU tasks by using a two-model setup, where the first bias-boosted model leverages confidence as an indication of biasness and then uses reweighting or PoE to debias the main model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

The approach is simple and sensible. It is known that models find it easy to learn/exploit biased samples thus obtaining high confidence on them. This method leverages that to learn a bias-boosted model which can then debias main model.

**Weaknesses:**

[W1] The paper claims that BiasPAD functions ‘without any prior knowledge’, but that seems to violate the no-free lunch theorem. BiasPAD actually relies on the knowledge that high confidence scores are indicative of label-aligned biases (i.e., bias-prone samples) and uses this ‘prior knowledge’ to debias the method. The claim should be narrowed down e.g., the model does not use ‘explicit bias annotations used by many prior works’.

[W2] While not exactly the same, I think the paper is highly related to “Learning from Failure” (LfF) paper [1]. LfF proposes an objective that boosts/amplifies bias of bias-only model to help debias the main model. Since this paper is also about boosting the bias, LfF should be cited and compared (experimentally + conceptually).

[W3] The work suffers from some of the flaws highlighted in [2]. That is, the empirical setting is non-comprehensive. It focuses only on two language tasks, with limited sources of bias. More recent works test on vision/language/vision+language problems with multiple forms of biases, which is a more realistic scenario.


[1] Nam, Junhyun, et al. "Learning from failure: De-biasing classifier from biased classifier." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 20673-20684.

[2] Shrestha, Robik, Kushal Kafle, and Christopher Kanan. "An investigation of critical issues in bias mitigation techniques." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision. 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity/Quality:**

The paper lacks clarity in terms of structural/grammatical issues at certain places.

Examples:
- Section 4.2 takes a very long time to specify how the bias score is specified. I think the top of Section 4 could just say ‘we leverage the fact that bias-prone samples have higher model confidence and use that to debias models’. 

- It does not define ‘golden label’ when it is first mentioned

- This description is very convoluted: “the sampled subset Dk will contain more biased samples after each step, meaning a more biased model Fb will be learned based on Dk according to our first observation, which in turn, a more biased model Fb will have more confidence in identifying the biased samples (according to our second observation) therefore increases the weights for the more biased samples for the next step”

**Novelty:**

To establish novelty, the paper should cite LfF (and perhaps other related papers) and distinguish itself. I think exact procedure of boosting bias is different, but the underlying principle is a well known one.
content.summary_of_the_review: I am voting for a rejection since the paper does not have enough contributions in terms of method development, new insights and experiments to be accepted at ICLR. However, given its simplicity, I do feel like this is a useful contribution for practical applications.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: More discussions about your concerns
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments, and we would like to address some of your concerns.

1. "The paper claims that BiasPAD functions 'without any prior knowledge',  but that seems to violate the no-free lunch theorem." 

The statement "without prior knowledge of any known biases" means that our bias-only model does not require any known biases. We don't think this goes against the no-free lunch theorem. We'll go through the article to identify ambiguities that might affect your understanding and fix them.

2. "While not exactly the same, I think the paper is highly related to the “Learning from Failure”  paper."

Apart from this article, many recent debiasing articles [1] [2] are based on this structure, and we have not considered this structure as our innovation.
Since our method is more focused on the NLP domain, we have compared it with methods in the NLP domain using a technique similar to the one you mentioned, and we achieved results that far exceed this method.
So we don't think comparing LfF on our task is necessary experimentally.
However, we will cite this article for a more comprehensive citation.

[1] Prasetya Ajie Utama, Nafise Sadat Moosavi, and Iryna Gurevych. Towards debiasing NLU models
from unknown biases.
[2] Victor Sanh, Thomas Wolf, Yonatan Belinkov, and Alexander M Rush. Learning from others’ mistakes: Avoiding dataset biases without modeling them.

3. "More recent works test on vision/language/vision+language problems." 

Our paper focuses more on the language field, and we have seen articles in the same field published in ICLR in recent years, so we think this article has the ability to be published in ICLR. 
Of course, we will also try on the general domains in the future.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: They proposed to "progressively and automatically detect and filter the biased data to train a robust debiased model" under the two critical assumptions that 'the higher bias rate, the more biased model' and 'the more biased model, the higher confidence in predicting the bias.' Mainly, NLU tasks are performed to evaluate relative performance gains against baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
#### **Strength**

- They assumed that the bias label is unavailable, practically considering an in-the-wild debiasing setting.
- A simple algorithm to debias reasonably performs

#### **Weakness**

- **W1. This work does not consider recent works.** In references, there is no paper in 2021, while having just one paper in 2022, which is briefly mentioned along with a paper in 2019 (Sec. 2). This work seems to shun the recent progress on debiasing methods and approaches. Please see the novelty in the review for details.

- **W2. Hyperparameters.** The boost step K, subset size n, and moving average coefficient $\lambda$ are critical hyperparameters for working. How do you find the hyperparameters not overfitting training data? Could you confirm that you found the hyperparameters using train/val splits? Although Sec 6.2 discusses K, how do you validate the generalization since you verify the results based on the MNLI-dev dataset? Does it occur overfitting? Does it generalize to other datasets? This issue should be handled more seriously and carefully.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
#### **Clarity**

- Figure 1 could be improved its clarity. Are the *strings of labels* prefixed to the hypotheses for label-consistent and label-conflicting samples?

#### **Novelty**

In Sec. 3, the insight into debiasing architectures is not appealing since there are a few papers that are already exploited (Nam et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2022). Although these works mainly focus on image classification tasks, we could readily apply them to NLU tasks. If the authors argue that their method has some different advantages, it is necessary to show in validation firmly.

- Nam et al., Learning from failure: De-biasing classifier from biased classifier. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33, 2020.
- Lee et al., Learning debiased representation via disentangled feature augmentation. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 34, 2021.
- Hwang et al., SelecMix: Debiased Learning by Mixing up Contradicting Pairs. ICML 2022: Workshop on Spurious Correlations, Invariance and Stability, 2022.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this work embraces two critical issues, significance and novelty. Due to the lack of key references, this paper seems to be not updated to reflect the related works in 1-2 years. Experimental validation is weak since the authors do not carefully discuss possible overfitting due to increased hyperparameters from the proposed bias-progressive training.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
For two sentence pair classification tasks (NLI and fact verification) for which biased (wrt cheating features) datasets are known to exist, the authors propose BiasPAD, a technique for training "biased feature presence" estimators which can be used during training a dual-sentence model in either the example reweighting (ER) or product-of-experts (PoE) framework to train a debiased sentence pair classifier.

The method basically involves iteratively training a "bias-only" (I would clarify this to mean specifically trained on single sentences if this is what you mean, see **Weaknesses** in next box) classifier and using model confidence as a proxy for degree of bias exhibited by the sample. They demonstrate that using confidence as a proxy is well-founded in a preliminary experiment using synthetic data. At the end of an iterative process which involves continuously updating the samplewise estimate of exhibited bias at each step, a samplewise "presence of bias" estimator is produced.

Using the aforementioned PoE, the authors then train a BERT-base model (for both bias presence estimation and pair classification) on MNLI and FEVER, and test on HANS, MNLI Hard, and two FEVER difficult subsets. For most of these test sets, their method outperforms the baselines significantly, with the exception of HANS Ent which is maximized by a standard model trained on MNLI (by design, as it is designed to be a challenge set where samples are overclassified as entailment when trained only on MNLI.)

The authors then provide an interesting analysis. In particular I appreciate their evidence that the bias-only model produced via BiasPAD outperforms other bias learning techniques using ROC.

### Missing References

**[1] M Saxon, X Wang, W Xu, WY Wang, *PECO: Examining Single Sentence Label Leakage in Natural Language Inference Datasets through Progressive Evaluation of Cluster Outliers* arXiv 2022**

```
@misc{saxon2022examining,
  url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09237},
  author = {Saxon, Michael and Wang, Xinyi and Xu, Wenda and Wang, William Yang},
  title = {PECO: Examining Single Sentence Label Leakage in Natural Language Inference Datasets through Progressive Evaluation of Cluster Outliers},
  publisher = {arXiv preprint},
  year = {2022},
}
```

**Rationale**: For section 2 **Debiasing Methods**: *data-centric methods*: You mention that the debiased datasets produced through sample removal or augmentation continue to exhibit bias, the following citation comprehensively demonstrated this on datasets including (Gururangan et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2019; Wu et al. 2022). Please include as support for the claim "While promising, the researchers also showed that the newly constructed datasets are hardly bias-free..." in NLI.



**[2] D Kaushik, A. Setlur, E. Hovy, ZC Lipton, *Explaining the efficacy of counterfactually augmented data.* ICLR 2020**
```
@inproceedings{kaushik2020explaining,
  title={Explaining the Efficacy of Counterfactually Augmented Data},
  author={Kaushik, Divyansh and Setlur, Amrith and Hovy, Eduard H and Lipton, Zachary Chase},
  booktitle={International Conference on Learning Representations},
  year={2020}
}
```
**Rationale**: They also attempt to produce a debiased dataset based on IMDb and SNLI

**[3] Y. Nie, A. Williams, E. Dinan, M. Bansal, J. Weston *Adversarial NLI: A New Benchmark for Natural Language Understanding.* ACL 2020**
```
@inproceedings{nie2020adversarial,
  title={Adversarial NLI: A New Benchmark for Natural Language Understanding},
  author={Nie, Yixin and Williams, Adina and Dinan, Emily and Bansal, Mohit and Weston, Jason and Kiela, Douwe},
  booktitle={Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics},
  pages={4885--4901},
  year={2020}
}
```
**Rationale**: another NLI dataset that was produced to attempt data-centric debiasing, should be included.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- Winning results on HANS and other benchmarks over the other comparison methods
- Their method requires no prior knowledge or assumptions about the bias apart from which sentence population (s1 or s2 in **missing citation [1]**) for MNLI and FEVER but otherwise presumably automatically finds sources of bias
- Supplementary experiments strongly demonstrate that their bias-condition model trained under bias-progressive training: 
    - acquires known (and probably unknown) biases better than simple fine-tuning on the dataset containing biases alone does based on AUC
    - is well-founded to be based on the model confidence heuristic (as Figure 3 shows via synthetic dataset experiments that show probability mass for the dev samples exhibiting the synthetic bias is strongly concentrated in high model confidence)


### Weaknesses
- This is a pretty specific problem, this paper might be better suited to a *ACL venue. I am personally not inclined to reject the paper on this basis however, provided they address the other weaknesses.
- I only understood the bias condition language in the paper clearly because I am familiar with this area, please ensure that in Section 4.1, 4.2 you clearly state that the bias only model is definitively learning a bias-only signal by being trained on only a single sentence in the population, (perhaps using "single-sentence" or "premise-only" language) rather than just saying "bias-only" as "biased" both refers to the premise sentence population as a whole and to the quality of certain samples which are individually exhibiting bias.
- Needs citations to support the problems for data-centric debiasing (see missing reference [1] in summary of paper section) and as examples of further important data-centric debiasing attempts (reference [2-3])
- Needs a grammar check (verb agreement issues, extra "the"s) for example:
    - p1: "reveal that the models tend to capture" -> "reveal that models tend to capture"
    - p2: "a higher the proportion of bias" -> "a higher proportion of bias"
    - p7: "which is verified to be enough to convergence;" -> "which is verified to be enough to converge;"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality is strong. Novelty is acceptible. Reproducibility and Clarity are acceptable, both based on the phrasing issue in Strength and Weaknesses.

### Novelty impact from missing references
Please add the aforementioned missing references.

### Vagueness in reference to "bias-only"
This is the only major weakness in the way the paper is written in my opinion. I have mentioned it at multiple places in the review already; just please make it clear that you are able to force a bias-only learning process for FEVER and MNLI by training on only a single sentence population. Non-NLP readers at ICLR may not be familiar with this issue and the unique paired-sentence nature of these tasks that makes training a bias estimator so straightforward.

**If you address these issue I will have more confidence in the appropriateness of this paper for the venue and will raise my score.**
content.summary_of_the_review:
**Overall this is a *high-quality* submission that, with some small changes, will be a strong addition to the ICLR 23 program.**

Please make the following changes:
- Fix clarity/reproducibility issue of "bias-only" language (specify which sentence population you mean when you train a bias-only model for each dataset, make it clear that by "bias-only model" you mean training on only a single sentence) in and around section 4
- Grammar check to clean up the stray "the"s throughout the paper
- Add missing references
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to the comments
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments, and we would like to respond to the following concerns.

1. "This paper might be better suited to ACL venue. " 
Since we have seen articles [1] in the same field published in ICLR in recent years, we think this article has the ability to be published in ICLR.
But we still appreciate your comment, and we will try it.
[1] Victor Sanh, Thomas Wolf, Yonatan Belinkov, and Alexander M Rush. Learning from others’ mistakes: Avoiding dataset biases without modeling them.

2. "Please ensure you clearly state that the bias-only model is definitively learning a bias-only signal."
Because our bias-only model is not limited to a certain type of bias (such as hypothesis-only bias), we use bias-only to name it. Thanks for pointing this out, we will refine this in the subsequent updates to reduce the ambiguity. 

3. "Needs citations to support the problems for data-centric debiasing and needs a grammar check." 
Thanks for your suggestions. We will fix the above issues in future versions.
